item.title: AnyLanguageModel 1.0 and Swift SDKs Enable Flexible Local and Hosted AI Inference
item.description:
AnyLanguageModel 1.0 and Swift SDKs Enable Flexible Local and Hosted AI Inference

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products, and today the ecosystem gains a new set of tools.

🔍 Overview

Apple’s Swift ecosystem now includes AnyLanguageModel 1.0, swift‑huggingface 1.0, and swift‑xet 1.0. After a year of development and dozens of releases, the new stack supports both local and hosted inference, a shared API, and the Foundation Models API so developers can pick the model that fits each task.

🛠️ How it works

  • A shared API lets you swap between system models, open‑weight models (llama.cpp, MLX, Core ML), and hosted providers without changing session code.
  • Tool calling works with every provider, supporting nested @Generable types and arrays.
  • Image support uses Foundation Models 27 syntax, allowing images to be attached to prompts on iOS, macOS, and visionOS 27.
  • Reasoning is now part of the transcript; when you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted if the new provider cannot replay them.
  • API keys are supplied via a closure rather than a static string, enabling apps to fetch short‑lived tokens from their own server.
  • The same Swift code runs on Linux, so you can use AnyLanguageModel on a server as well as on Apple devices.

⚙️ Key details

  • Local vs. hosted inference: Both are supported, and hosted providers receive the same capabilities as local models—guided generation, streaming tool calls, and token‑usage reporting.
  • Supported platforms: iOS, macOS, visionOS 27, and Linux.
  • Model compatibility: On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel works with any model conforming to the Foundation Models LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.
  • Accelerated downloads: swift‑huggingface and swift‑xet bring fast model downloads from the Hugging Face Hub directly into Swift apps.

Model sizes and requirements

Model Format Approx. Size Runtime notes
GGUF (Q4_0) GGUF ~3.4 GB Quantization‑aware training
GGUF (Q4_K_M) GGUF ~1.7 GB
Qwen3.8 27B (MLX) MLX ~16 GB (4‑bit) Fits on a Mac with ≥32 GB memory
GLM‑5.3 (Z.ai) BF16 ~1.5 TB Requires four maxed‑out Mac Studios

🚀 Availability

  • AnyLanguageModel 1.0, swift‑huggingface 1.0, and swift‑xet 1.0 are released and ready for integration.
  • Hosted model support has been expanded this year; the same features available to local models are now offered by inference providers.
  • Migration guidance is provided in the release notes for each package to help developers update existing apps.
  • Community feedback and contributions directly shaped several major features; contributors are thanked for making AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

💡 Why it matters

  • Developers can now choose the most suitable model—small local models for quick on‑device starts or large hosted models for heavyweight tasks—without rewriting code.
  • The unified API lowers the barrier to experimenting with different providers and capabilities such as tool calling and image‑augmented prompts.
  • Upcoming additions include “models that decide” and “models that listen,” extending the range of capabilities reachable through the same Swift‑first workflow.

#FoundationModels #SwiftAI #LocalInference #HostedAI

Source: AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

item.title: Moku Brings Mobile Vibecoding Workspace for AI Agents to Multiple Platforms
item.description:
Moku Brings Mobile Vibecoding Workspace for AI Agents to Multiple Platforms

Moku, a pocket‑sized coding workspace for AI agents, is now available across iOS, macOS, Android, Linux and Windows, letting developers code from a phone or tablet with a full‑featured terminal experience.

🔍 Overview

  • Moku is a thoughtfully designed pocket workspace: a fast mobile terminal plus a coding workspace for your AI agents.
  • The goal is to make mobile vibecoding a daily habit, replacing hours spent tethered to a desk with a keyboard and mouse.
  • It is not traditional remote software; it delivers a delightfully crafted interaction, refined developer experience, polished UI, and exceptional performance.

🧩 How it Works

  • Runs locally in your browser; there are no real connections and no real commands.
  • Moku embeds Tailcat, the userspace networking tool from Tailscale’s open‑source stack.
    • Run tailcat --serve=22 on the host, paste the short token into Moku, and the two ends establish an encrypted peer‑to‑peer connection.
    • The link falls back to DERP relays only when necessary; there is no port forwarding, no relay VPS, no root required.
  • Native Mosh keeps the shell alive through Wi‑Fi ↔ 5G handoffs and elevator rides.
  • On iOS, the Dynamic Island and Lock Screen show your agent’s state through the mascot’s eyes.

⚙️ Key Features

  • A simulated server is already connected.
  • Pick a coding app, expand a project, and drop into a conversation right on the same page.
  • Moku lists every open pane at the top of the drawer with its current task; you can peek in read‑only or take the keyboard with a single tap.
  • On connect, Moku scans the host for on‑disk projects and sessions from 12+ coding CLIs: Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Qoder, Trae, Kimi, Grok, MiniMax Code and more.
  • Selecting a project and tapping its session reopens it inside a real terminal with full context.
  • Moku’s Rust core parses ANSI at 2.1× the throughput of common emulators and paints a 10 MiB log burst in about 0.3 s.
  • Multiple agents can run side by side on one host (e.g., Herdr runs several agents such as pi exploring, grok implementing, codex chasing a root cause).

🚀 Availability

  • Free on every platform.
  • iOS: available on the App Store and via a public TestFlight beta.
  • macOS: ships through TestFlight.
  • Android: Universal APK and per‑ABI builds downloadable from GitHub Releases.
  • Linux & Windows: Native packages (.deb / tarball for Linux, Windows installer) on GitHub Releases.
  • Not listed in mainland China yet — the App Store link requires a non‑CN Apple ID.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Classic mobile SSH clients (e.g., Termius, Blink Shell, Prompt) were designed for emergency sysadmin commands; Moku was built from day one for mobile vibecoding and AI agents.
  • Zero‑config private networking works without public IPs or router configuration.
  • One‑tap resume for Claude Code, Codex and other agents enables developers to code anywhere, turning a phone into a usable development terminal.

#Moku #AIAgents #MobileCoding #Vibecoding

Source: Moku — Pocket terminal & coding workspace for the AI-coding era

item.title: Google launches Guided Vision in Gemini Live for real‑time audio descriptions on Android
item.description:
Google launches Guided Vision in Gemini Live for real‑time audio descriptions on Android

Google’s Guided Vision feature debuted today in the Gemini Live app on compatible Android devices, providing real‑time audio descriptions of anything pointed at with the phone’s camera.

🔍 Overview

  • Guided Vision works when you share your camera in Gemini Live.
  • It delivers spoken information about small text, surroundings, objects, and details on specific items.
  • Users can ask follow‑up questions, such as reading an expiration date.

🧩 How it works

  • The phone’s camera feed is processed by Google’s Gemini AI, which generates audio cues to help line up the shot if the target is off‑frame.
  • The system is designed for people who are blind, have low vision, or need situational assistance, similar to Apple’s VoiceOver Live Recognition.

⚙️ Key details

  • Reading fine print – the AI can read small text and fine print.
  • Object identification – it can find or identify objects in the scene.
  • Follow‑up queries – users can ask additional questions about what they see.
  • Audio alignment cues – Gemini provides cues to adjust the camera view.
  • Safety disclaimer – Google advises not to rely on Guided Vision for navigation, safe‑travel guidance, obstacle detection, or as a substitute for a cane or mobility aid.

🚀 Availability

  • Integrated in the Gemini Live app.
  • Also available through Google TalkBack.
  • Can be enabled via an accessibility shortcut in the Settings app on Android 9 and above, following recent Pixel updates.

💡 Why it matters

Guided Vision extends AI‑powered visual assistance to Android users, offering a new way for low‑vision individuals to access information about their environment without additional hardware.

#Google #Accessibility #AI #GuidedVision

Source: Google’s new Guided Vision feature can help you read the fine print
